title: The Treasures of Sutton Hoo

paragraphs.text: The Anglo-Saxons were a mix of tribes from areas that are now part of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands who settled in England between about 410 and 1066 AD. The presence of artificial hills, created as burial mounds and known as tumuli, is an obvious sign that Anglo-Saxons inhabited an area. In the late 1930s, Edith Pretty, owner of Sutton Hoo House in Suffolk, England, commissioned a local archaeologist, Basil Brown, to investigate a large tumulus on her land. However, while examining it, Brown saw that a trench had been dug into its centre and he assumed that, in the distant past, it had been robbed of its treasures. He decided to explore the smaller surrounding tumuli instead. Having found nothing in them, he turned his attention again to the large tumulus. He discovered the outline of a boat which was 27 metres in length. Although the wood of the ship had long ago disintegrated, at its centre was a burial chamber packed with artefacts that were in remarkably good condition. It became apparent that the robbers had for whatever reason stopped digging just centimetres away from a spectacular hoard of treasure.

This find gave historians their first opportunity to see the sort of objects that a powerful and wealthy man of the seventh century owned. The magnificence of Sutton Hoo not only revealed the surprisingly exotic artistic tastes of Anglo-Saxon nobility, but also encouraged a major re-evaluation of the period, and a realisation that Anglo-Saxon culture was neither primitive nor lacking in sophistication. For some time, the assumption was that the individual buried in the tumulus was a king of the English region of East Anglia. This was due to the fact he had such magnificent riches all around him. But historians now believe that robbing burial sites was a common occurrence during the period. This suggests it is quite likely that many of the tumuli that are empty today were once packed with treasure like the one at Sutton Hoo. Historians now believe the individual buried there may not have been royalty; he might have been any of the wealthy individuals in Anglo-Saxon society who had access to highly skilled craftsmanship. The discovery was also significant because so few artefacts from the Anglo-Saxon period had been found up to that point. Although the Anglo-Saxons left some manuscripts and coins, and a few examples of their architecture, compared with all subsequent eras there had not been much to see.

This all changed with the discovery of Sutton Hoo. To the right of where the body was buried was a set of spears and a magnificent sword, 85 centimetres in length. Along the west wall of the chamber, a large circular shield was found, largely composed of gold along with some copper alloy and also some red gemstones known as garnets. The front of the shield has two striking designs – a large predatory bird and a flying dragon. It closely resembles shields excavated by archaeologists in Sweden, but this one is thought to have been produced in East Anglia and is considered to show a higher standard of craftsmanship. One of the most famous discoveries was a helmet made of iron. This again seems to be based on designs found in Sweden, but was the work of Anglo-Saxon craftsmen in England. It had been shattered into hundreds of fragments and so had to be reassembled by experts. The design features a long snake reaching down to touch the beak of a bird.

Close to the legs of the buried man were various drinking vessels made from the horns of an animal, the auroch, which is now extinct. A large dish measuring three quarters of a metre across, and with handles, was also discovered. This is made of pure silver and was almost certainly manufactured in Serbia. It features a woman's head and is artistically comparable to dishes produced in the later days of the Roman Empire.

Another important find was a purse which would originally have hung from a belt. Although the bag itself, which was made of leather, has disintegrated, the ornamental purse lid has survived intact. It was made of gold and garnets and was adorned with artwork depicting wolves. The purse had contained 37 gold coins; interestingly, these were not a local currency but were Frankish. The coins were crucial in determining that the burial almost certainly took place in the 620s. Another important discovery was a set of ten bowls made of silver and with the design of a cross on each one. It is thought that these were the work of craftsmen in Egypt in the 7th century AD. Spoons were found close to the bowls and have names inscribed on them.

The treasures of Sutton Hoo show us that this corner of Suffolk was extraordinarily well-connected to the wider world. Much of the craftsmanship was clearly influenced by, or the result of, Scandinavian work. After seeing these finds, it is impossible to think of early Anglo-Saxon society as being cut off or culturally isolated; instead, it is obvious that it should be considered part of a wider European society stretching from the Mediterranean to the North Sea.
